analysis.one_liner: Makes Social Security and railroad retirement benefits fully exempt from federal income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or any cosponsors; it died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the tax code so that no one pays federal income tax on Social Security retirement benefits or Tier 1 railroad retirement benefits. Today, retirees whose income from pensions, savings, or wages is high enough must pay tax on up to 85% of their benefits; this bill would repeal that rule starting the year after enactment. To protect the Social Security trust funds, the bill would also order the Treasury to replace from general federal revenue any money the trust funds lose because benefits are no longer counted as taxable income.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and disability beneficiaries who pay federal income tax on their Social Security benefits — typically those with income above about $25,000 for singles or $32,000 for couples from pensions, savings, or wages. A retired couple in that group could keep several thousand dollars a year that currently goes to the IRS. Lower-income beneficiaries who already pay no tax on benefits would see no change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpaying Social Security and railroad retirees

how_it_helps.text: Excludes Social Security title II retirement benefits and Tier 1 railroad retirement benefits from gross income entirely, and repeals the existing tax rule on those benefits [S2] [S3].
Includes workers' compensation amounts that substitute for reduced Social Security benefits, so no one loses the exemption by receiving a substituted benefit [S3].

Requires the Treasury to replace from general revenue any reduction in transfers to the Social Security trust funds and the railroad retirement account, so the trust funds themselves are held harmless [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury and, ultimately, general taxpayers. Taxes on benefits now flow partly into the Social Security trust funds; the bill replaces that money from general revenue, and repeals the tax entirely, so the lost income tax revenue is not offset by any other tax increase or spending cut.

drawbacks.text: The tax exemption is worth the most to retirees with substantial other income, because lower-income beneficiaries already pay no tax on their benefits; the largest dollar gains would go to higher-income households [S3].
The bill repeals the existing tax without any offsetting revenue, adding to federal deficits unless other taxes are raised or spending is cut elsewhere [S3].

Social Security's combined trust fund reserves are already projected to be depleted within roughly the next decade under current law; adding a permanent general-revenue transfer of this size would deepen that long-term financing problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a retiree currently taxed on benefits, the gain is real and immediate. The cost is broad and long-term: the money is not replaced by any other source, so the exemption adds permanently to federal deficits while slightly favoring better-off retirees over lower-income ones. The bill never addressed these trade-offs, since it never received a hearing or amendment process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee took no action, and the Congress ended with the bill never having a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gosar introduced the bill on July 16, 2021 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No cosponsors joined from either party [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one had to weigh the trade-off; the tax on benefits stayed as is, and the federal Treasury kept the revenue it would have lost. Beneficiaries who pay tax on benefits are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; taxed beneficiaries saw no change

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 16, 2021 and took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill and no member of either party cosponsored it, so no party took a position.

industries.industry: Higher-income retirees with pensions and savings
industries.note: They would stop paying income tax on benefits they already receive; the gain is largest for those with the most other income. Lower-income beneficiaries would gain nothing because they are not taxed now.
The bill permanently removes benefit tax revenue and adds a standing general-revenue transfer to the trust funds with no offset, raising deficits unless taxes or spending change elsewhere.
